Easy: Create a function to calculate the positive and negative sentiment of a set of text with a time dimension using the tm package. Plot the positive and negative sentiment over time.

I would like some help about this task. I have used a sentimeal dictonary to get the setment of each word on text.
Then I have analysed some text books for a period of time. I mean I get a collection of books from 1970, 1971 and 
so on. After all,  I plot the graph for each year. Is this what the task is about? I may get it wrong?

Thanks for the help

messages.author: 1c8b9e31e3450098
messages.subject: Re: Sentometrics
parts:
Hi Gustavo,

Sentiment analysis is not easy. The same word or phrase can have vastly different sentiment depending on its context and factors about its situation which may not be evident from the text. The idea of plotting sentiment as a function of time requires a detailed history of each term with dates, and that is in no way easy, because there are tens of thousands if not hundreds of thousands of such terms you might want to cover.

Would your proposal be better suited to improving R's existing sentiment analysis, whether in the tm package or elsewhere? Seth Grimes is holding this symposium and may be able to suggest possible co-mentors if your revised proposal meets with approval of the mentors:

http://2017.sentimentsymposium.com/

Who knows, maybe Seth wants to co-mentor. He's certainly well-connected. The only way to find out is to ask him so I've cc'ed him. I would be happy to co-mentor if an already-invited mentor would like to mentor. I have plenty of NLP experience, but the other R mentors are skeptical of my appreciation of adjusting symbolic regression for actual model degrees of freedom and my distaste for the size of the finance sector, so who knows whether they will let me this year.

If you want an easy task, how about using the new Google Trends API as a complement to sentiment analysis in the tm package? Here is a JavaScript snippet which uses the new Google Trends API to get the past week of information about the Making Work Pay tax credit:

https://runkit.com/58cc73351463760015f5f3a5/58cc73351463760015f5f3a6

That would be great to have in R's tm package, and it's easy but you would still need multiple passes for comparable outputs, because Google does some kind of de-normalization leaving the y-axis indeterminate, but scaled around the range 0-100. Why they don't use logarithms instead is beyond me.

Best regards,
Jim
